More about setup, execution and approval +

Setup and changes

LLMs help engineers create reusable functions, constraints, tool adapters and test scripts. New projects, PDKs or tool requirements may need adjustments. AI-assisted circuit requests and exceptional repairs can use model calls.

Routine execution

Once configured, code generates supported layouts, calls EDA tools and collects results without LLM calls. Explicit steps and criteria make repeated runs reviewable. Code can contain errors, so its outputs still need checks.

Approval

DRC checks geometry; LVS compares connections. Run applicable electrical simulations, resolve issues and review evidence for the actual design version before acceptance.

THE QUESTIONS THAT MATTER

What runs?
What gets checked?
Who stays in control?

The distinction is simple: the LLM helps create the framework. The framework executes the routine work. Engineers approve the results.

How is this different from an agent doing the work?+

Our LLM use is concentrated on building or adjusting the framework: reusable functions, tool connections, constraints and test scripts. In a configured routine run, code executes those steps instead of asking an LLM to decide each action. This describes our approach; other products may also combine agents and reusable code.

What does “framework” mean in practice?+

It is the reusable code and configuration that connect the design steps: device and PDK adapters, placement and routing functions, constraints, tool calls, tests and result collection. A new project can reuse it, with changes where its requirements differ. The proposed project extends the current layout flow into digital design, verification and integrated chip implementation.

Why not let an LLM control the whole run?+

Repeated engineering work needs consistent constraints, required checks and clear acceptance criteria. Putting those steps in code makes them explicit and reviewable. It also avoids repeated LLM decisions during routine execution. Code can still contain errors, so the outputs must be checked.

Does normal execution use LLM tokens?+

The configured routine layout flow runs through code and EDA tools without LLM calls or token use. AI-assisted circuit generation, setup changes and exceptional repairs can still use model calls. Compute and EDA-tool costs remain separate.

Where do expert-designed circuits and layouts fit?+

The planned library pairs curated circuits with expert-designed layouts to support framework development and validation. Historical project data would be included only with the owner’s permission. Library implementation, data access and any model-training use are not yet confirmed.

Which PDKs can I use on the cloud?+

The cloud setup includes SKY130, GF180MCU and IHP SG13G2. Choose a supported catalogue circuit or supply a compatible netlist for the selected process, then generate a layout and inspect the available checks. The recording on this page uses SKY130; circuit and device support depends on the selected PDK.

How can another PDK be adapted?+

The team has outlined a cell-export approach, using TSMC as an example:

  1. InstantiateCreate the required PDK cells in Cadence.
  2. GenerateUse the PDK’s parameterised cells to generate layouts.
  3. ExportFlatten the cell layouts and export the geometry.
  4. ReuseBuild a palette of prebuilt cells for KLayout.

A local Mistral Small instance could help write scripts for the export steps. A geometry palette is one part of adaptation: device models, connectivity, extraction and process-specific checks must also be integrated. Adaptation service availability is being confirmed.

Does “DRC clean” mean the chip is finished?+

No. DRC checks geometry against the rules being run. LVS compares extracted connections with the reference circuit. Electrical performance, reliability and manufacturing sign-off require the applicable simulations, checks and expert review. After an edit, rerun affected checks on that design version.

What if the automated flow fails?+

Investigate the failed step, make a bounded repair and rerun the relevant checks. AI may help diagnose an unfamiliar problem; unresolved issues go to a specialist. A failure is part of the evaluation, not a result to hide or automatically approve.

Who can use it, and can designs stay private?+

The intended users include students, independent chip builders, small companies and professional design teams. Use shareable examples in the public trial until access controls, retention and data-use terms are confirmed. Private workspaces, stored feedback and opt-in contributions are planned. The notes feature on this page downloads a file locally; it does not upload designs or feedback.

What hardware are you developing next?+

The proposed accelerator will perform inference for a selected language-model or image-processing task used in chip development. It will combine established compute, memory, interfaces and control blocks. Workload-aware power management is the priority improvement. The first model, architecture, process and numerical targets remain to be selected.

Why start with power management?+

The team’s experience includes DC-DC converters, LDOs and mixed-signal design. We will profile the selected workload to identify where energy and time are spent, then assess compute and memory activity alongside power-delivery losses. The comparison will include the added control circuitry, task quality and latency.

Will the chip use GlobalFoundries?+

GlobalFoundries is the preferred implementation route. The exact process, PDK access, device options and tool compatibility remain to be confirmed. The three cloud PDKs are available for supported layout examples; they do not by themselves establish the process for the future inference accelerator.

How will you demonstrate the benefit?+

For the design flow, record an initial implementation, a requested change and renewed verification. Count setup, engineering hours, model calls, reruns and review. For the accelerator, compare energy per completed inference, latency, throughput and area at the same task quality. Include memory, interfaces and power-delivery losses within the stated system boundary.

Where would the cost savings come from?+

From reducing repeated specialist work and, where suitable, commercial EDA licence spending. The comparison must include setup, compute, integration, failures and engineer review while meeting the same requirements. The team estimates that design is roughly 40–50% of a programme’s total cost. Programme savings therefore equal the net design-phase saving multiplied by that share. For example, a hypothetical 20% saving across design would mean about 8–10% off total programme cost. The layout/DV share within design and measured savings still need to be established.
